To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the prognostic impact of genetic alterations is highly dependent on the context; (2) genetic alterations are not mutually exclusive, but can occur concurrently; (3) genetic alterations can be associated with specific histologic subtypes; and (4) genetic alterations can occur in different histologic subtypes, thus blurring the boundaries between histologic subtypes.
(i) BRAF mutation is associated with aggressive behaviour and poor outcome, and (ii) TERT promoter mutation is associated with distant metastasis and reduced survival.
BRAFV600Emutation is associated with a better outcome, whereas RAS mutations and TERT promoter mutations are associated with a worse prognosis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of genetic markers that may help in predicting the behaviour of the tumour, in order to guide the patient towards more aggressive treatment.
the identification of genetic markers with a prognostic value in surgically resection thyroid carcinoma, which can guide the management of the patient and help to predict their outcome.
a better understanding of genetic markers and their clinical significance, and with the identification of new markers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the genetic landscape of well-differentiated thyroid carcinomas is complex, and the genetic profile of a single patient may be influenced by the presence of other genetic lesions, by the microenvironment, by the stage and extent of disease and by other factors.
the genetic landscape of thyroid carcinoma, although still under investigation, is far from being simple and that the prognostic value of genetic alterations is still to be fully understood.

, in well-differentiated thyroid carcinomas, the prognostically most important genetic alterations (BRAFV600E and RET/PTC) are also those that can be detected by molecular methods, thus suggesting that the genetic alterations that are most relevant for the patient's outcome are the ones most easily detectable by molecular methods.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the genetic profile of thyroid carcinomas is more complex than previously thought, with a large number of mutations being found in well-differentiated tumours.
, although genetic markers are useful to predict outcome, their clinical relevance should be interpreted in a wider perspective that includes morphologic and clinicopathologic factors.

the genetic landscape of thyroid cancer has been enriched with new markers that will be further explored to refine the prognostic and predictive value of the current staging and risk stratification systems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
genetic markers are not independent predictors of outcome.

the genetic profile of a thyroid cancer patient is only one piece of a larger puzzle that also includes morphological, immunohistochemical and (F)ish features as well as clinical and pathological context.
genetic markers, when used alone, have limited prognostic value, and their interpretation should be made in the context of the patient's overall disease and clinical status.
